before: {This is a familiar closure problem in turbulent-flow modeling. Resolving the smallest dynamically active scales is computationally costly~\citep{yang2021grid}, so practical models must account for their effects on the resolved scales. A common approach uses approximate dissipative closures, such as eddy viscosity or hyperviscosity, to represent transfer to unresolved scales. These closures can reproduce selected aspects of the flow, but their accuracy depends on the quantity and scale of interest. For example, in forced two-dimensional turbulence, viscous, hyperviscous, and Leith closures can approximate enstrophy transfer, whereas the Smagorinsky closure dissipates enstrophy at the wrong scales~\citep{pietarila2013closures}. Resolution studies provide a related caution: mean dissipation and enstrophy can be nearly converged while higher-order moments of velocity gradients, dissipation, and enstrophy, together with distribution tails, remain substantially underestimated~\citep{DonzisResolutionEffects}. Reproducing bulk statistics therefore does not ensure accurate fluctuations or extreme events.}

before: {A complementary approach allows the closure to depend on the history of the resolved state. Unresolved variables have their own dynamics, so their influence need not be determined by the current resolved variables alone; past observations can contain information about those hidden degrees of freedom. The Mori--Zwanzig formalism makes this explicit: eliminating unresolved variables generally yields an instantaneous term, a history-dependent memory term, and a term associated with unresolved initial conditions, even when the full dynamics are Markovian~\citep{YenTingLinMZ2021,de2026data}. Retaining the memory contribution leads to a \emph{non-Markovian} closure, in which the resolved evolution depends on past states as well as the present one. This motivates persistent temporal memory as a mechanism for representing unresolved influences that an instantaneous dissipative approximation may miss.}

Retaining memory leads to a \emph{non-Markovian} closure, motivating persistent temporal context for representing unresolved influences.}

We divide training into segments of 96 six-hour steps (24 days), processed as four consecutive 24-step windows. Both the SSM states and causal-convolution caches start at zero for each segment and are carried through all 96 steps. Each window begins with four teacher-forced steps using ERA5 inputs, followed by 20 steps using corrected forecasts as feedback. Meteorological inputs return to ERA5 at each window boundary, while temporal memory is retained with its gradient detached. Gradients propagate through memory within each window and are stopped through meteorological feedback. Figure~\ref{fig:training_segments} in Appendix~\ref{app:architecture_details} illustrates this procedure.

Policy names specify memory handling during training first and forecasting second. Carry/carry retains the updated SSM states and causal-convolution caches; reset/reset zeros both before every step, retaining all learned weights and the two-frame meteorological input. Every training segment and independent forecast begins with zero temporal memory under both policies. Table~\ref{tab:memory_controls} in Appendix~\ref{app:architecture_details} summarizes the policies. \vfourchange{The original SWA comparison uses one run per policy; the subsequent replication uses five carry-trained runs and one reset-trained run.}
